title: The oldest US data series in FRED
gist: The oldest US data series in FRED is federal public expenditures on public works, starting in 1791, while the oldest series overall is UK population data going back to 1086 (the next 41 oldest are also UK). The US series is dominated by the WWI military spending surge, is in unadjusted current prices with no price index old enough to deflate it, and was reconstructed retrospectively in 1920 with loose definitions.

insights.claim: The oldest data series in FRED is population data for the United Kingdom dating back to 1086, and the next 41 oldest series are also from the United Kingdom.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: For anyone needing multi-century macro history, the deepest FRED coverage is UK, not US — start there when building very long-run baselines.
insights.quote: the oldest series in FRED is population data for the United Kingdom, dating back to 1086!
insights.locator: FRED has not only current data series

insights.claim: The oldest United States series in FRED is federal public expenditures for public works, with observations going as far back as 1791, and a couple of other public-expenditure categories also start in 1791.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: 1791 is the practical floor for US fiscal time series in FRED — anything claiming deeper US history is coming from outside this dataset.
insights.quote: Our FRED graph above shows data on federal public expenditures, specifically for public works, that go as far back as 1791.

insights.claim: FRED's full catalog can be re-sorted by observation start date: from the Categories page choose "All Series," then switch "Sort by Popularity" to "Sort by Obs Start" to surface the longest-history series.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A reusable discovery recipe for finding the longest-running series in any category instead of only the most popular ones.
insights.quote: change “Sort by Popularity” on the right side of the listing to “Sort by Obs Start.”

themes.theme: What the 1791+ US expenditure series actually shows

insights.claim: The chart of US federal public expenditures since 1791 is visually dominated by the huge increase in military expenditures that came with World War I.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Wartime spikes swamp everything else in nominal long-run fiscal series — rescale or log-transform before reading peacetime trends.
insights.quote: The graph is dominated by the huge increase in military expenditures that came with WWI.
insights.locator: The graph is dominated by the huge increase

insights.claim: A small bump in the US federal expenditure data in 1904 corresponds to the purchase of the Panama Canal and surrounding land: $40 million paid to France and $10 million to Panama.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Individual one-off asset purchases are large enough to move the whole series in this era — treat single-year moves as event-driven, not trend.
insights.quote: the little bump in 1904 corresponds to the purchase of the Panama Canal and land around it: $40 million to France and $10 million to Panama.
insights.locator: For example, the little bump in 1904

themes.theme: Caveats on using very old data

insights.claim: The 1791-onward US federal expenditure data are in current prices — prices at the time, not inflation-adjusted — and no price series exists that is old enough to deflate them.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Real-terms comparisons across this history are impossible within FRED; any nominal-vs-nominal comparison across centuries is misleading.
insights.quote: the data are calculated in current prices—that is, prices at the time, which have not been adjusted for inflation. And there’s no price series that is old enough to help reconcile this issue.
insights.locator: Note that the data are calculated in current prices

insights.claim: The oldest US expenditure data were computed retrospectively in 1920, so collection practices were not up to modern standards and some liberties appear to have been taken with the definitions of the data.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Treat pre-1920 US fiscal history as a retrospective reconstruction with definitional drift — usable for narrative, weak as a precise quantitative benchmark.
insights.quote: the data were computed retrospectively in 1920, which means that the data collection practices used were obviously not up to modern standards. In fact, it seems some liberties were taken with the definitions of the data.
insights.locator: Indeed, the data were computed retrospectively
